description: With no GPS on Mars and up to 22-minute signal delays to Earth, astronauts cannot rely on remote mission control. MartisDux solves this by unifying scattered orbital data into an offline mission guide. It layers terrain, slope hazards, and science targets onto one map, while using AR and VR for 3D tabletop route planning and virtual walks. Complete with landing simulations to test safe touchdown zones and local logging for field records, it helps crews explore Mars safely and autonomously.
summary:
MartisDux is an open-source project that makes Mars feel navigable. Decades of orbital and rover data exist, but answering simple questions about one place (how steep a slope is and whether you can get there) still means digging through archives never meant to be read together. With no GPS on Mars and radio delays of up to 22 minutes, explorers will need those answers close at hand.

MartisDux brings them into one layered map: terrain and elevation, routes, scientific sites and hazards, drawn over the same ground. A working prototype already combines USGS elevation data, Perseverance’s real traverse and its sample sites.

All official maps, AR experiences, navigation and hardware integrations will be built and tested in our desktop simulator for Windows and macOS. Every layer is cited and transparent about its limits, because tools for reading public mission data should be open too.
details:
MartisDux puts Mission Control on board a Mars mission. From Mars, a question to Houston and its answer take up to about 22 minutes. A suit leak or a solar storm won’t wait that long. MartisDux is a desktop app for Windows and macOS that makes the flight controller’s main calls itself, using NASA and partner data:

  • whether a planned Marswalk is GO or NO-GO;
  • the fastest way home the moment something goes wrong.

1. A layered Mars globe. The app opens on a 3D Mars built with CesiumJS. You can switch between:

  • Viking colour, CTX, 1 m HiRISE imagery and THEMIS infrared
  • MOLA relief
  • the USGS geologic maps: the global map (SIM 3292) and the detailed Jezero crater map (SIM 3464, 1:75,000)

You can search places or coordinates, browse landmarks, and open real Perseverance and Curiosity 360° panoramas. A live clock shows the current Earth–Mars radio delay.

2. Slope hazards and safe routes.

  • Slope map: for Jezero and Gale, the app computes slope from NASA’s 1 m HiRISE elevation models and colours the ground as easy (under 10°), caution (10–20°), steep (20–30°) or no-go (30° and above).
  • Route planner: a terrain-aware planner, running in a background thread, finds the safest walking route between two points. It refuses ground steeper than the walking limit (25° by default) and never cuts diagonally past a no-go cell.

3. The Marswalk plan. The app turns a route into a full suited-walk plan:

  • Walking time: the Tobler hiking function, scaled so that level ground matches a suited walking speed of 0.9 m/s
  • Energy: the Pandolf load-carriage equation, corrected for Mars gravity (3.721 versus 9.807 m/s²). Defaults are a 75 kg crew member, a 70 kg suit and 10 kg of tools
  • Oxygen: derived from that energy
  • Radiation dose: from Curiosity’s RAD measurement of 0.64 mSv per sol
  • Daylight: the Sun must be at least 10° above the horizon, using NASA’s Mars24 algorithm
  • Suit budget: 8 hours with a 45-minute reserve that can’t be spent.

4. The walk-back guarantee. This is the core safety feature, modelled on how Apollo 15 planned its traverses.

  • The app runs a shortest-path search over every cell of the terrain around base: 669 × 672 cells at Jezero, in under a second. The result is the fastest walking time home from anywhere
  • At every point on the way out, time already spent plus time to get home must fit inside the suit budget
  • The first point where it doesn’t is reported as the point of no return
  • The same field is drawn as 30-minute rings on the map
  • Poll: before a walk, the app checks route, ground, suit, way home, daylight, solar storms, body and radio, just as a flight director polls each controller
  • Live walk: during the walk, a console tracks the crew’s position along the timeline
  • 6. Storm shelter map.
  • Method: for every point, the app computed the horizon angle in 36 directions and the share of the sky that terrain hides. Cliffs and buttes give partial cover from solar particle events.
  • Live forecasts: NASA’s DONKI service supplies forecasts of solar storms arriving at Mars.

7. Ground truth built in. Rover check overlays the slope map’s test against Perseverance’s real measured tilt (results under Benefits).

8. Traverse sheet and discovery log.

  • Traverse sheet: the route gets numbered stations. Each shows its USGS rock unit and a real Perseverance photo, matched to the rover’s location counter. The sheet saves as a one-page PDF.
  • Discovery log: records observations with a Mars position. Ship to Houston simulates sending them, with a countdown at the real light time.

9. Life-size walk with a helmet display.

  • Ground: you stand at the Perseverance landing site at 1:1 scale. The walkable 2 × 2 km uses NASA’s native 1 m HiRISE elevation with 0.32 m-per-pixel imagery. Beyond it, coarser measured data (CTX, HRSC/MOLA, Viking) continues out to the crater rim and the horizon
  • Visor: shows heading, the steepest slope found in an 80 m scan, elevation, turn cues and the live storm forecast. Suit values are clearly labelled SIM. Anything without data behind it says “Unknown”
  • Devices: it runs as a desktop preview, on Android in AR and in VR headsets. The phone and headset versions haven’t been tested on real devices yet
  • Tabletop model: a 3D model of the walk area can also be placed on a desk through a phone’s AR viewer

10. Works offline.

  • Bundled data: everything the app needs ships with it: terrain, rover data and weather records
  • Tile cache: map tiles you view are kept on the device, up to 2 GB.
  • Pack this walk for offline: downloads every image tile over a route ahead of time.

That matters because a crew on Mars can’t count on an internet connection.

The simulator’s role. MartisDux’s website presents this app as the simulator where official maps, AR experiences, navigation routes and hardware integrations are built and tested before use.

What benefits it has

Decisions without waiting for Earth. Every safety call (GO/NO-GO, point of no return, way home in an emergency) is computed on the device in milliseconds, so the radio delay doesn’t matter.

Honest about uncertainty. Every value is labelled measured, derived or simulated. Missing data shows as “Unknown”, never as zero. DATA-SOURCES.md records each dataset’s source, method and limits, down to file checksums.

One tool instead of many archives. Imagery, elevation, geology, rover photos, weather records and space weather sit on one map with the same coordinates. Answering “how steep, what rock, can I get there and back” no longer means digging through separate archives.

Useful for more than astronauts. Mission planners can compare routes. Researchers can see what was measured where. Students can look inside every number.

The intended impact

Safer first crewed walks on Mars. MartisDux aims to show that the planning discipline of Apollo (walkback and rideback limits) can be computed on board for Mars, where Mission Control can’t answer in time. It makes the decisions a crew needs in an emergency fast, explainable and tied to real data.

Better maps after every walk. The team’s follow-up proposal, The Suit as a Sensor, closes the loop:

  • What: small tilt and pressure sensors in the astronaut’s boots check the map with every step.
  • Why: an orbital map is a forecast of the ground and can be wrong at the scale of one step. Small ledges, soft sand like the sand that permanently trapped the Spirit rover in 2009, and changes since the image was taken all fall below its resolution.
  • How: the app compares each measured step with what the map predicted and warns at once when the ground is steeper or softer than the safe limit. Every reading is kept to correct the map for the next crew.
  • Status: this is a proposal. No hardware has been built.

Open knowledge. Mars data was gathered by public missions, so the tools that read it should be open too. The team plans to publish the code, methods and data sources so anyone can check a map, fix it or build on it.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Languages:

  • JavaScript (ES modules): the app and the website.
  • Python: data preparation and validation (NumPy, requests, pyogrio, pyproj, shapely, Pillow).
  • GLSL shaders: 3D effects on the website.
  • HTML and CSS.

App:

  • CesiumJS 1.146: the 3D Mars globe and terrain.
  • three.js 0.183: the life-size walk and the helmet display.
  • Electron 44 and electron-builder: the desktop app. It produces a portable Windows .exe, a Windows installer, and macOS packages for Apple Silicon and Intel. The app window runs sandboxed, with context isolation on and Node access off.
  • Vite 8: build tool.
  • Node.js: local tile server and device tile cache.
  • Web Workers: route and walk-back searches without freezing the screen.
  • Service worker: offline storage of the whole app.
  • Google model-viewer: tabletop AR on Android and iPhone.
  • WebXR: life-size AR and VR.
  • LERC: decoding elevation data.
  • qrcode-generator: sending the walk to a phone.
  • Node’s built-in test runner: the automated tests.

Website (MartisWeb):

  • Vite and vanilla three.js: a WebGL Mars planet; a cinematic loading screen in which the camera dives through an astronaut’s visor, with a 3D starfield that reacts to the pointer; and real Jezero data in the layer and explorer sections.
  • Hosting: Vercel.

NASA and partner data:

  • JPL Mars Trek: Viking, CTX, HiRISE, THEMIS, MOLA and geology tiles.
  • Elevation: NASA/USGS 1 m HiRISE elevation models for Jezero and Gale.
  • Geology: USGS geologic maps SIM 3292 and SIM 3464.
  • Rover data: Perseverance and Curiosity traverses and tilt records (NASA MMGIS), the raw images feed, and 27 sealed Perseverance sample sites.
  • Weather: Curiosity REMS weather records, 4,745 sols binned by season.
  • Space weather: NASA DONKI (WSA-ENLIL arrival forecasts at Mars).
  • Orbits: JPL’s approximate orbital elements for the radio delay.
  • Clock: the Mars24 algorithm for Mars time.

Other tools: git and GitHub for version control and releases, the Khronos glTF Validator for the 3D models, and Google Drive for distributing the app.

Hardware:

  • Built so far: developed and run on ordinary Windows and Mac laptops. The AR walk targets ARCore Android phones and VR headsets, though those haven’t been tested on devices yet.
  • Proposed: boot sensors (a phone-grade tilt chip and a pressure-sensing insole, with ground-contact sounding as a longer-term research idea).

How the project is creative

Mission Control on board. Most Mars maps show you the ground. MartisDux makes the flight director’s calls: GO/NO-GO, point of no return, walk home now. It treats the map as a decision tool for a crew cut off from Earth.

Apollo planning applied to Mars. The walk-back field turns Apollo 15’s walkback and rideback limits into a live map showing how far from home you are, in minutes, from every point.

Terrain as a radiation shelter. Computing how much sky the terrain hides, then checking the result against the RAD team’s measurement at a real butte, is an unusual use of elevation data. It turns cliffs into places to shelter from solar storms.

Rovers as test pilots for the map. The team used rovers’ own tilt sensors to grade the slope map, which is rarely done in student projects.

A judge’s idea, made physically possible. A judge suggested sonar on the astronaut’s feet. Sound barely carries in Mars’s thin air, so the team kept the goal and swapped the sensor for tilt, pressure and contact sounding.

Real ground at life size. You can stand at the Perseverance landing site at true scale on real 1 m elevation, with a helmet display that only shows what has data behind it.

A memorable first impression. The website’s loading screen dives through an astronaut’s visor into the site, setting the tone before any text is read.

Factors the team considered

Safety and conservative choices.

  • An 8-hour suit budget with a 45-minute reserve that is never spent.
  • A 25° walking limit.
  • Walk-back times that always use the slower uphill speed.
  • Drills based on reported events, such as NASA’s account of particles from the May 2024 storm reaching Mars “in just tens of minutes”.
  • Planning numbers are clearly called estimates, not flight rules.

Scientific honesty.

  • Every dataset is cited, with method, resolution and limits.
  • Values are marked measured, derived or simulated.
  • Display choices are labelled and can be switched off: ×2 height exaggeration on the life-size walk, illustrative pebbles near the walker, and tinted monochrome images.
  • Known gaps are stated, such as rocks and ripples smaller than the 1 m data.

Validation. Claims are tested against independent ground truth and the tests are published. Each limit is written down, for example that rover tilt validates the terrain model, not whether a person can walk there.

Data resolution and coverage. The 1 m data covers only small areas, so the app blends finer and coarser layers. It shows where coverage ends and avoids inventing detail.

Coordinates. Datasets use different map projections and longitude conventions. The team aligned them so the same point lands in the same place on every layer, and the map, the walk and AR share one set of coordinates.

Offline use and the radio delay. Everything runs on the device. Live feeds fall back to their last saved copy, labelled with its age.

Performance. Heavy searches run in background threads. Tiles are cached on disk with a size limit. The website loads heavy parts only when needed and adapts quality to the device.

Usability. Following lessons the team drew from past NASA Space Apps winners: short labels, visible layer switches, coordinate input and a clear map → pin → destination → route → save workflow. Explanations sit in Data and Help instead of crowding the screen.

Security. The desktop window is sandboxed and isolated from the system.

Accessibility. The website supports reduced motion and keyboard navigation and describes images for screen readers.

Credit and licensing. NASA, USGS, JPL, the University of Arizona, MSSS, ASU, ESA/DLR and others are credited. Open-source licences (CesiumJS, fonts, LERC) ship with the app. The one AI-generated illustration is labelled as decoration.

Cross-platform distribution. Windows (portable and installer) and macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) builds are available. The README notes that the builds are unsigned, so Windows may show an “unknown publisher” warning.

Feasibility of the hardware idea. The team checked that the boot sensors exist today (phone-grade tilt chips, insoles used for gait analysis). It identified the open problems: cold down to about −100 °C at night, abrasive dust, calibrating how far a boot sinks, and false alarms when a foot lands on a rock. It also set out a build order: a simulated boot in the app, then a phone strapped to a shoe, then a pressure-insole test on sand.
